source: Sinha, Arun, Goel, Staab, Geiping (2025) The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs
finding: Gap 3. When the plan and knowledge are given, models still fail on long runs because they condition on their own earlier errors. Wrong state carried in context makes later steps worse.
numbers: Qwen3-32B, best of the open models tested, falls below 50% task accuracy within 15 turns although first-step accuracy is near perfect. Injecting 0/25/50/75/100% wrong past turns lowers accuracy at turn 100 in proportion. Larger models self-condition at least as much (even frontier non-thinking: DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2, Qwen3-235B). Qwen3 thinking mode removes the effect. Single-turn horizon: GPT-5 2176 steps, Claude-4 Sonnet 432, Grok 4 384, Gemini 2.5 Pro 120.
quote: models become more likely to make mistakes when the context contains their errors from prior turns
limits: Synthetic running-sum task (key-value retrieval and addition), not a natural reasoning task. Markovian task, so history can be dropped; real tasks have long-range dependencies.
agent_relevance: A restated state is only safe if it is rebuilt from checked facts, not copied from the agent's own earlier restatement. An S2 restatement that inherits an earlier error will lock it in (self-conditioning). Supports re-deriving state from source each step.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) Illusion of Diminishing Returns, Appendix C.1-C.2 (self-verification and context engineering)
finding: Gap 3 and 5. Telling a model to self-verify does not fix self-conditioning. Cutting the model's view of its past turns (sliding window) does help.
numbers: Self-verification prompt: fixes self-conditioning only partly, causes overthinking in thinking models and uses more tokens per turn in CoT models. Sliding context window: accuracy rises as the window shrinks (Fig. 10a compares 1-turn window, 25-turn window and majority vote N=10).
limits: Window result holds for Markovian tasks without long-range dependencies. Exact per-window accuracies are in a figure, not read as numbers.
agent_relevance: Re-stating the current state compactly and dropping old turns is a tested mitigation; a verify-yourself line alone is not.

source: Shojaee, Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Horton, Bengio, Farajtabar (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Gap 3. Frontier reasoning models collapse to near-zero accuracy beyond a complexity threshold on puzzles, and giving the exact algorithm in the prompt does not move the collapse point.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi, Checker Jumping, River Crossing, Blocks World. With the algorithm supplied, the collapse happened at roughly the same N. A Claude 3.7 Sonnet (thinking) run is near-perfect at Hanoi N=5 (31 moves) but fails River Crossing at N=3 (11-move solution). Collapse persists at temperature zero (appendix).
limits: Contested: critiques say output-token limits and unsolvable instances explain part of it. Sinha et al. attribute the failures to execution. Not a test of explicit state restatement.
agent_relevance: Failure of long multi-step state tracking is real in frontier models; knowing the rule does not suffice. Tells against trusting a single long chain with no state checks.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Gap 5. Without outside feedback, asking a model to review and correct its own earlier answer does not help and often hurts. The apparent gains in earlier work came from using the true label to decide when to stop.
numbers: Oracle label stops correction: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5. Intrinsic correction (no oracle): GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0; GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 and 43.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (2023) only. Prompts for the critique step matter; later models and training may differ.
agent_relevance: A same-model self-check of a restatement is weak evidence of error detection. Check against the source text or an independent pass, not a rereading by the same context.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Gap 5. The bottleneck of self-correction is finding the mistake, not fixing it. Given the true error location, correction works well.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 CoT traces from PaLM 2 Unicorn, first logical error annotated. GPT-4 overall mistake-finding accuracy: 39.80 (trace-level prompt), 52.87 (direct step-level), 43.40 (CoT step-level). GPT-4-Turbo 30.13 and 48.33; GPT-3.5-Turbo 10.44, 14.78, 14.31. With a given error location, backtracking improves downstream accuracy on all 5 tasks (a trained classifier for location also helped).
limits: Errors are in PaLM 2 traces, not the checker's own output. Checkers were 2023 models. Task types are word sorting, shuffled-object tracking, logical deduction, multistep arithmetic, Dyck.
agent_relevance: Criterion (c) misrepresentation detection: a model finds a flaw in a reasoning chain about half the time at best. A scaffold should give locating hints (which slot, which source line) rather than ask 'is this wrong?'.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Gap 5. Larger models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false when the format is right, and can score P(True) for their own sampled answers; P(IK) probes work in-domain but calibrate poorly on new tasks.
numbers: Abstract-level reading only: P(True) AUROC axes about 0.6-0.85 across tasks in the figures; self-evaluation improves when the model sees many of its own samples. No single headline number extracted.
limits: I read the abstract and figure labels, not every table. Pre-2023 models. Calibration is on answers, not on restated problem representations.
agent_relevance: A cheap self-confidence signal exists and improves with several samples, but it measures answer validity, not whether the S2 restatement matches the problem.

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Gap 5 and 7. A biasing feature in the prompt (for example the correct answer always placed at option A in few-shot examples) shifts answers, and the written chain of thought rationalises the biased answer without naming the bias.
numbers: Accuracy drops by as much as 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks with GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0. Social-bias task: explanations justify stereotyped answers without mentioning the bias.
quote: CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction
limits: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 only. 'As much as' is the maximum drop, not the mean.
agent_relevance: A stated representation can be a plausible story that does not reflect what drove the answer: stated content is not proof of use. Argues for tests that edit the restatement and see whether downstream steps change.

source: Shi, Chen, Misra, Scales, Dohan, Chi, Scharli, Zhou (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Gap 7. Behavioural test of distractor failure: irrelevant sentences added to maths problems cut accuracy. Self-consistency recovers a lot of it, but not all.
numbers: GSM-IC. code-davinci-002 COT micro accuracy 72.4%, macro accuracy (all variants of a base problem right) 6.0%. LTM micro 77.5%, macro 18.0%. 0-COT micro 29.0%. Adding an ignore-irrelevant instruction: COT 77.8%, LTM 80.6%. Self-consistency (20 samples): COT 88.1%, LTM 93.4% micro; LTM+SC macro 45%; 0-COT SC gain 35.5 points. Correct answer is within 20 samples for 99.7% of problems. For more-than-2-step problems some distractors drive text-davinci-003 macro accuracy to 0.
limits: 2022-era models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003). Arithmetic only. Self-consistency is majority vote, not an internal-agreement signal like CCS.
agent_relevance: Agreement among samples helps against distractors in behaviour (unlike CCS probes in Farquhar). But even the best method keeps macro accuracy at 45%, so more than half of base problems still fail somewhere. Restating only the relevant quantities in S2 is a form of the 'ignore irrelevant info' fix.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen, van Steenkiste (2025/2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Gap 8. LLMs asked to keep a belief about a hidden user preference over five rounds barely improve after round 1; a normative Bayesian assistant does far better. Fine-tuning on Bayesian assistant outputs closes much of the gap and transfers.
numbers: Flight recommendation, 624 simulated users, 5 rounds, 100 new test sets per round. Final-round accuracy of the Bayesian Assistant 81%; off-the-shelf models (Gemma 2 9B/27B, Llama 3 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 7B/32B, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro) about 36-58% and plateau after round 1; chain-of-thought, numeric formatting, 30 rounds and base models gave no meaningful improvement. Bayesian-tuned LLMs agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time and beat oracle teaching. Humans (48 users) improved more than most LLMs but fell short of Bayesian.
limits: Figure values read from garbled text; per-model numbers approximate. Gain comes from fine-tuning, not prompting; the paper reports prompting with CoT did not help. Single synthetic domain with transfer to hotels and web shopping.
agent_relevance: A single best-guess state is what prompted LLMs keep; weighted hypotheses are not produced by CoT alone. A scaffold that stores explicit weighted hypotheses and updates them in code or by rule is a candidate; not tested here at equal tokens.

source: Hu, Lu, Zhang, Song, Lam, Zhang (2024) Chain-of-Symbol Prompting for Spatial Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Gap 1 and 4. Replacing natural-language intermediate steps with condensed symbolic state (objects and relation symbols) raised accuracy and cut tokens in spatial planning, with the same number of demonstrations.
numbers: Brick World 1D, GPT-3.5-Turbo: 31.8% (CoT) to 92.6% (CoS), +60.8 points; input tokens reduced by up to 65.8%. SPARTUN real spatial QA, 5-shot: GPT-3.5-Turbo 47.1 to 49.4; GPT-4 69.8 to 72.6; intermediate tokens 198 to 167. Total test set 5,500 instances (4,000 Brick World). Three runs with different demonstrations.
limits: Only GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4 and Llama-2 tested (authors' own limitation). Gain shrinks sharply on the more natural benchmark (+2.3 and +2.8 points). Symbol format is task-specific; token counts are for demonstrations. Not a typed-slot ablation.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for gap 1: a more structured, compact state beats free-text steps for GPT-3.5, but the gain is small for GPT-4 on natural tasks. Expect big effects only where free text is ambiguous.

source: Kim and Schuster (2023) Entity Tracking in Language Models
finding: Gap 1. Tracking the state of entities through a list of state-changing operations (boxes and objects) works in-context only in the GPT-3.5 models, which were pretrained on code, not in text-only GPT-3 or Flan-T5.
numbers: Box-and-object task; accuracy measured per box after n operations. Only the GPT-3.5 (code-trained) models succeed; GPT-3 davinci, instruct variants and Flan-T5 base/XL do not beat copying the initial state. In the Alchemy data, copying the initial state is right 62.7% of the time, so baselines matter.
limits: 2023 models; exact accuracies per operation count are in a figure. Fine-tuned small T5 can learn the task but does not generalise to new surface forms.
agent_relevance: State tracking is a trained capability, linked to code pretraining. A scaffold that writes state in code-like typed form uses what these models are good at.

source: Prakash, Shapira, Sen Sharma, Riedl, Belinkov, Rott Shaham, Bau, Geiger (2026) Language Models Use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
finding: Gap 6 and 8. Causal mediation and interchange interventions on Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3-70B and Llama-3.1-405B show a mechanism for character beliefs: binding each character-object-state triple with ordering IDs and retrieving it by lookback; a separate visibility ID updates one character's view of another.
numbers: Models: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Llama-3-70B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct. Dataset CausalToM (two characters, two objects). Interchange intervention accuracy shown by layer in figures; exact IIA values not extracted.
limits: Open-weight models up to 405B, simple stories, causal evidence rather than probes alone. Not frontier closed models. IIA numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Causal (intervention) evidence that an LLM keeps per-agent belief state with pointer-like structure. Supports typed per-agent slots in S2, with the caveat that this is simple story data.

source: Zhu, Zhang, Wang (2024) Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
finding: Gap 6 and 8. Linear probes read the belief status of the protagonist and of the oracle (the other agent) from attention-head activations in Mistral-7B; pushing activations along the belief direction changes false-belief task scores.
numbers: Probes above 75% validation accuracy on a subset of heads (null 75%, binary chance 50%, four-way chance 25%). Intervention along the protagonist-minus-oracle direction (+TpFo) raises Forward Belief 'both' accuracy to about 0.97 against about 0.68 for a random-direction control in the table (table layout garbled in extraction; confirm in the paper).
limits: Mistral-7B and a second 7B model only. Table rows scrambled by PDF extraction, so exact baseline unclear. Intervention effects are task-specific.
agent_relevance: Intervention shows consumer use, not just decodability, for belief states in a 7B model. Does not show it for frontier models.

source: Yuan and Sogaard (2025) Revisiting the Othello World Model Hypothesis
finding: Gap 6. Seven language models (GPT-2, T5, BART, Flan-T5, Mistral, LLaMA-2, Qwen2.5) trained on Othello moves learn to play and learn similar board representations, judged by cross-model alignment.
numbers: Up to 99% accuracy in unsupervised grounding between models' final-layer representations; synthetic-data move generation error rates fall with model size and data; GPT-2 and T5 reach 99.6 on one 1-hop synthetic metric in Table 2.
limits: This is representation similarity across models, not a causal intervention, and says nothing about whether frontier prompted models hold board states. It does not address Vafa et al.'s coherence failure. Models are trained on Othello, not general LLMs.
agent_relevance: Supports convergence of structure across architectures for a rule-governed domain; does not settle use or coherence.

source: Slocum et al. (2025) Believe It or Not: How Deeply do LLMs Believe Implanted Facts?
finding: Gap 9 (fine-tuning vs prompting contrast). Belief depth is tested three ways: generalisation, robustness, and probe similarity. A fact put in the system prompt works for generalisation but collapses under scrutiny; synthetic-document fine-tuning (SDF) holds up on most facts.
numbers: Base model Llama 3.3 70B Instruct; methods: prompting (20 system prompts written by Claude 4.5 Sonnet), AlphaEdit mechanistic editing, SDF; four fact-plausibility categories; judge Claude 4 Sonnet. Prompting and SDF generalise to downstream tasks, causal implications and Fermi estimates; mechanistic editing does not. Under adversarial system prompt, critique task and four-turn debate, prompting and editing fail and SDF persists except on egregiously false facts (one case: open-ended belief 80% to 50% under compute-controlled training on 2k documents).
limits: Facts implanted, not representations of a task. LLM-judge scoring. Open-weight base model. Not a test of selection-history grounding but is the closest prompt-versus-training contrast found.
agent_relevance: Training-grounded states persist under pushback; prompt-stated states do not. An S2 restatement made by prompting is likely shallow and needs checks, as a teleosemantic reading would predict.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Causal Theories of Mental Content (primary-source cross-check)
finding: Gap 9. Confirms the origin and form of the disjunction problem and the roles of Fodor and Dretske.
numbers: Fodor 1984 'Semantics, Wisconsin Style' states the disjunction problem: why 'X' means dog and not dog-or-blow-to-the-head. Fodor 1987 Psychosemantics gives asymmetric dependency. Dretske 1981 information semantics; Dretske 1988 Explaining Behavior adds function (teleoinformational).
limits: Secondary source; the original books by Fodor and Dretske were not opened. Quoted wording is SEP's.
agent_relevance: Gives the correct basis for using 'disjunction' in notes: a state caused by several things does not fix what it is about, which maps to restatements that bundle distinct hypotheses.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Teleological Theories of Mental Content (primary-source cross-check)
finding: Gap 9. Confirms Swampman and functional indeterminacy objections and that selection can include learning, not only evolution.
numbers: Davidson 1987 introduced Swampman; on standard etiological theories Swampman's states have no content. Fodor 1990 frog case: fly vs small-dark-moving-thing are equally adaptive contents. Millikan 1984 allows meme selection; Papineau 1984 speaks of learning; Dretske 1986 uses recruitment by conditioning; Garson argues neural selection counts as selection. Non-etiological views (for example Nanay's modal view) avoid Swampman.
limits: Secondary source. Millikan, Dretske and Block originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports Mollo and Millière's move that training counts as selection. A fine-tuned model has a selection history; a prompted state has none, which matches d15.

source: Mollo and Millière (2023) The Vector Grounding Problem
finding: Gap 9. The paper argues an LLM's internal states can be grounded if they carry causal-informational relations and have a selection history; post-training with human preferences is the strongest case and the pre-training objective a weaker one.
numbers: No experiment and no numbers. Section 6.2 defends the selection premise with three strategies: post-training (instruction tuning and RLHF), pre-training next-token prediction, and a third. Uses Millikan, Neander and Shea for teleosemantics, Wright 1973 for function.
limits: A philosophical argument; no testable prediction is stated by the authors. The text searched did not use the words Swampman or disjunction.
agent_relevance: The fine-tuning-versus-prompting contrast is the only empirical handle; d15 is a loose test. No direct test of selection-history grounding was found.
